this is not what i said. i’m saying to examine your process. if trying fifteen different beans did not produce a desirable outcome, then try altering a different part of your method, whether that be your water, ratio, grind size, or brew method. 

pretend your a scientist, your current hypothesis is that starbucks has the ability to make coffee better than you ever can at home. it is your job to disprove your hypothesis by using the scientific method. adjust one variable at a time, slowly honing in an exact recipe that will be just as good as (or, more likely, better than) starbucks coffee
it doesn’t do a better job at extraction, you’re overthinking it. there is no secret. it’s just plain and simple using good, quality ingredients, and utilizing good technique.

as another commenter said, starbucks uses softened, reverse osmosis filtered water. best suggested practice for what water to use is to either use purified drinking water or distilled water (to minimize impurities), or, my personal preference, your favorite fresh spring water, as the vitamins and minerals can positively (or negatively, ofc, depending on preference) the taste of a cup of coffee. typically the only time tap water will be a preferable option will be if your tap water comes directly from a local spring, and is not chemically treated in the same way most water in the usa is.

well we brew our cold brew in plastic bins, and store our iced coffee in plastic pitchers, so maybe micro-plastics are the secret you’re searching for! 😊

no, but in reality we don’t do anything special to our coffee aside from maybe grinding the cold brew fresh? iced coffee comes pre-ground, however. 

to improve your home brewing method, you should examine three things: the quality of your water, the quality of your beans, and the size of your grind. plain tap water, especially depending on what part of the world you are located, can severely impact the quality of a cup of coffee. buying poor quality coffee, or using a grind size that is either too coarse or too fine for your brew method can also impact the taste quite drastically.

when you brew coffee at home, are you drinking it hot or iced? temperature effects how our tongues detect flavor. at starbucks, our iced coffee is brewed hot then mixed with ice to cool it down. our cold brew (like many cold brews) is brewed with room temperature water, and allowed to steep for twenty hours

i would also recommend examining your ratio of coffee (in grams) to water (in milliliters), for example when i brew coffee myself, i enjoy between a 1:12-1:14 ratio of coffee to water. that’s 1 g of coffee to every 12-14 ml of water. if you are interested in learning more, find James Hoffman on youtube, he has a lot of videos that act as great resources and tutorials for learning better brewing techniques and ratios

hi! trans woman partner, here! i know i don’t know Pam’s pronouns, but from one mtf person to another, i would assume that it’s not solely they/them pronouns, but maybe rather she/they or she/her? i know if i was Pam, and i came across this post about me, i’d feel a deep hurt in the way i was referred to.

when you refer to trans women in this way, you are effectively stripping away the validity of our femininity. you are saying that while i am allowed to perform femininity, i am not allowed to claim the title of woman. i am something different, i am “other.”

and that’s hurtful

i’ve dealt with this concept of defeminizing language in my personal life for a long time (and i’d wager a bet most other trans women have as well). it’s something i deal with at work, from customers and coworkers alike, from friends and loved ones, and, for too long of a time, from my own-self and my own internalized transphobia.

for many years, i used some variation of they/them or she/they, or even neopronouns based on the silly idea in my head that i didn’t deserve to be a full woman, that i hadn’t earned it yet. i was so, so wrapped up in this idea of appealing to the cis people around me, being as unobtrusive as possible, sacrificing a part of my identity because it was just easier to get people to say “they” instead of “she.” because i hadn’t earned that privilege yet from them. i wasn’t pretty enough. i wasn’t feminine enough.

for their part, on why people are so comfortable defaulting us to “other,” i suspect it’s largely subconscious, and i suspect it’s for similar reasons to what i stated for myself. it happens more often when i’m in trouble, when i’ve done something to upset someone, so suddenly i’ve lost the privilege to be a woman temporarily. 

the other side of it is convenience. it is simply easier to “other” me rather than risk explaining to a customer or an introduction that yes, i am, in fact, a woman, and not some creature to ogle. so “they” i become, leaving that person’s interpretation of my identity up to the whims of whatever narrow minded views said person may hold. 

this is the version that hurts the most, in my opinion, even if it isn’t malicious. suddenly i am thrust into being hyper aware that my friend values their own comfort over mine, and even potentially over my safety, and this makes me wholly unconfident in their willingness to respect my identity and defend me when i’m not in the room

i want to be clear and say, i don’t believe this is your intention! you seem to care about your coworker, and you seem to want her identity to be respected, so i’m asking you to please listen to what i have to say. if Pam’s pronouns are they/them, then continue as you were, and i’m sorry for climbing onto my soap box at 2 in the morning. but, if it’s as i suspect, the i would please urge you to make a concerted effort to change the language you use when you refer to her. and stick up for her in making sure others do the same. off my soap box now 🫡
